pun-thao.name: Pun Thao Kong A Shrine
pun-thao.lead: Connecting faith with the old port district

then.headline: A shrine from the Chinese community in a mining port
then.body:
Official records from Takua Pa Town Municipality state that Bun Tao Kong Shrine was the first shrine in the town. It is located in the old port district known as Chap Se. This places the shrine within the picture of Takua Pa connected to maritime trade and the old market area. However, available documents do not provide a starting year or the name of an individual founder.

The Talat Yai Community Database notes that the founders were Chinese immigrants who came to mine tin in Takua Pa, mentioning various groups such as Hokkien, Hainanese, and Cantonese. This information makes the shrine both a ceremonial site and a spiritual anchor for the labor and merchant community in the mining town. Yet, there is no direct evidence to settle which group was the founder or what specific function the shrine served in the port system.

The municipality also records that inside the shrine is an incense burner bestowed by King Vajiravudh (Rama VI), which is a trace of the relationship between the local shrine and the Siamese state in the past. However, the year, occasion, or the object's travel history are not verified.

before.headline: An old shrine with gaps in its transition records
before.body:
From verifiable public sources, there are no records of the shrine ever being abandoned, changing hands, or restored in any specific year. There is also no declaration of it as a registered ancient monument. Therefore, such stories should not be filled in from the context of the old town or other shrines.

What is confirmed is that in 2021 (2564 B.E.), there were video recordings of the Sae Yid ceremony for the deity Hok Tek Chia Sin (Pae Kong) at the Pun Thao Kong Am Shrine in Chap Se. Another video mentions the oil bathing ceremony, the Phra La ceremony, and the invocation of sacred fire. This shows that the shrine was still a ritual space for the descendants of Takua Pa during that time.

As for whether the 2004 tsunami affected the building, or the results of the tin mining closure and the changing city economy, no sources have been found that mention this shrine directly. This remains a research gap, and it is not verified whether it was damaged or not.

now.headline: Still alive as a community shrine, but 2026 status data is incomplete
now.body:
The latest evidence found does not confirm official opening hours, caretakers, admission fees, or the building's condition in 2026. Therefore, it should not be stated that the shrine is open to tourists every day. Verified information shows that the shrine is in the Udom Thara Road area, Talat Yai community, and has a history tied to the old Chap Se port district.

In terms of community use, the 2021 videos show that Chinese ceremonies were held and descendants of Takua Pa returned to participate. The shrine thus still appears as a space of faith and shared community memory. However, there is no public evidence to confirm an annual event calendar or a management committee.

No news from the past five years has been found confirming any specific restoration projects, awards, or development projects for this shrine, and there are no current photos from official agencies with verifiable usage rights.

kue-chai.name: Kue Chai Tung Shrine
kue-chai.lead: Telling the culture of worship through the shrine's details

then.headline: From Mr. Ngo Chok's house to Takua Pa's first shrine
then.body: The starting point with the clearest evidence is not a year, but a community story: Mr. Ngo Chok bought house number 87 on Sri Takua Pa Road and converted it into a shrine, driven by faith after praying for tin mining yields and fortune. Another document refers to its original name as 'Thian Wan Keng' and its legal name as 'Kue Chai Tung'.

before.headline: The shrine grew with the mining town and became a community ritual space
before.body: The context of the shrine is tied to Hokkien Chinese who immigrated to mine tin in Takua Pa and brought deities from China to be enshrined. Local sources and travel media explain that the shrine is in the old market district, which has old buildings and a cultural street. It therefore serves as more than a place to pray: it is an anchor for the Chinese community and a space for the Vegetarian Festival.

now.headline: A northern shrine still alive during the Vegetarian Festival
now.body: The latest evidence found is NBT news published in May 2026 (2569 B.E.), which presents Kue Chai Tung Shrine, or 'Rong Phra Talat Nuea' (the northern market shrine), as a center of faith for Takua Pa people and states that it still preserves its original cultural identity. News of the 2023 festival also confirms that Kue Chai Tung Shrine participated in the Iu Keng ceremony, parading deities around the old town of Takua Pa.

rong-jae.name: The Shrine in the Garden
rong-jae.lead: A space of belief collectively maintained by the community

then.headline: An old shrine of the Chinese community in Takua Pa
then.body:
The Shrine in the Garden, or Seng Leng Keng Shrine, appears in the documents of Takua Pa Town Municipality as a century-old shrine. However, the same document does not provide a starting year of construction, so it cannot be pinned down to a specific reign.

The founder stated in the municipal document is Mr. So Thian Seng, an overseas Chinese. After the shrine was built, the deity Cheng Chui Cho Sue (the Dewdrop Deity) was invited from China to be enshrined. The place likely served as both a place of worship and a spiritual center for the Chinese community in the mining and port town of Takua Pa. However, the construction year, the founder's policy reasons, and its daily role in that era have no location-specific evidence.

Another local document says that Mr. So Seng previously worked with the Kue Chai Tung Shrine before opening the shrine in the garden. However, it is not verified whether this is the same person as Mr. So Thian Seng, so it is not presented as the same fact.

before.headline: A transition period with blank documents
before.body:
From verifiable sources, no evidence has been found that the shrine changed hands, was abandoned, or was restored in any specific year. There is also no specific evidence on how the 2004 tsunami affected this building.

No ancient monument registration list for the Shrine in the Garden has been found, and there is no information that it was ever converted into another business or public building. The verifiable information during this transition period is only the continuity of the place name and the memory of it being an old shrine. The history of other shrines in the old town district should not be borrowed to fill in the gaps.

The context of Takua Pa changed from a mining and maritime trade town to a historical and cultural town, but the sources found do not yet connect these city-level changes to specific events at the Shrine in the Garden.

now.headline: Still named in the Vegetarian Festival landscape, but operational status is unclear
now.body:
Currently, verifiable online sources do not confirm who the caretaker is, whether the shrine is open to visitors every day, what the condition of the building is, or if any restoration projects are underway. Therefore, it should not be written that it is open as a tourist attraction or can be visited without an appointment.

The contemporary evidence found is a review article reporting the sale of Ko Sui snacks at the Shrine in the Garden during the Vegetarian Festival. This information shows that the place is still used as a community activity spot during the festival. But this is a report from a blog, not the shrine's official schedule, and it does not confirm that the activity is held every year.

Travelers should use the address Soi Rong Phra, Rat Bamrung Road as a starting point and check with locals or the municipality before traveling, as there are still no verified coordinates, opening hours, phone numbers, or official contact channels.

highlights.detail: The deity that the municipality states is enshrined in the shrine. Also known as the Dewdrop Deity, it has a history of being invited from China.

highlights.detail: The Roi Jang blog reports that Grandma Tan Si Lun sells Ko Sui snacks at the Shrine in the Garden during the Vegetarian Festival. This is information from a blog that still needs to be verified for sales in the year of travel.

phra-narai.name: Phra Narai Park
phra-narai.lead: Rest in the park and continue with town history

then.headline: The park's origins remain behind a veil of evidence
then.body:
For Phra Narai Park directly, no documents have been found that specify the year of establishment, the initiator, or the reason for setting up the park. Therefore, it should not be concluded that the park was created during the tin mining era or the era of the town governors simply because Takua Pa town prospered during that time.

What is verified is that the park is located in front of the Takua Pa Town Municipality office and is the site where the statue of Phra Narai (Vishnu) and his attendant deities are enshrined. The Phra Narai deity has such meaning to the town that it is used as the municipal emblem. But this evidence explains the importance of the deity statue and the town, not the birth date of the park.

The context of Takua Pa town in municipal documents reflects an old town with trade, tin mines, Sino-Portuguese buildings, and a large Chinese community. However, there is still no evidence connecting these elements directly to the creation of the park.

before.headline: From a sacred space to a town activity stage
before.body:
The evidence found does not record the park changing hands, being abandoned, or being restored as a specific time period. It therefore cannot be concluded how the park transitioned through different eras.

What is found is a record in the municipal environmental operations plan (2020) that lists Phra Narai Park as a religious site. Activities held at this park that appear in news and local documents include the Takua Pa Old Town Sunday Market opening, the Vegetarian Festival (where the park is used as a gathering point for processions in some years), and the Phra Narai worship ceremony. This indicates that the park serves as both a place to house a symbol of faith and a public space for the town's contemporary cultural activities.

However, no evidence has been found on how the 2004 tsunami affected the park, nor any ancient monument registration by the Fine Arts Department for the park specifically (separate from the ancient statues).

now.headline: A public park in the 2026 context
now.body:
Although there is no news of a major park renovation in 2026, the continued use of the park for town events shows its active status. It remains a landmark for those coming to the Takua Pa Old Town Sunday Market, and the statues of Phra Narai and his attendants are still spots for faith and photo opportunities.

Travelers can use this park as a starting point to walk into the old town area, as it is located on Si Takua Pa Road, not far from the market and old buildings. However, specific facility details such as restrooms or wheelchair ramps in 2026 have not been confirmed by recent documents.

highlights.title: Phra Narai and attendant statues
highlights.detail: Replicas of the deities enshrined in the park. The originals are ancient sculptures from the Khao Phra Narai archaeological site, now in the Thalang National Museum.

highlights.title: Municipal symbol
highlights.detail: The Phra Narai image is used as the emblem of Takua Pa Town Municipality, reflecting the town's historical roots linked to Indian culture.

highlights.title: Proximity to the Sunday Market
highlights.detail: The park is a landmark near the Takua Pa Old Town Sunday Market, often used as an activity space or gathering point for festivals.

getting_there.text: Located on Si Takua Pa Road, in front of the Takua Pa Town Municipality office, in the old town area.

did_you_know: The Phra Narai statues in the park are replicas; the original ancient sculptures were moved for safekeeping at the Thalang National Museum in Phuket.
The Phra Narai image is the official emblem of Takua Pa Town Municipality.
